lesson.title: The Methyl Tag That Silences Genes
lesson.summary: DNA methylation is the enzymatic addition of a methyl group to cytosine bases, typically at CpG sites, and is generally associated with reduced transcription of the affected gene.
lesson.body:
DNA methylation is one of the best-understood epigenetic marks. An enzyme called a DNA methyltransferase attaches a small methyl group directly to a cytosine base, converting it to 5-methylcytosine. In mammals this happens overwhelmingly at CpG sites, meaning a cytosine immediately followed by a guanine in the same DNA strand. Note that the sequence itself is untouched, cytosine is still cytosine, so this fits the definition of an epigenetic mark: heritable, but not a change to the genetic code.

Many gene promoters contain stretches of DNA unusually rich in CpG sequences, called CpG islands. When a promoter's CpG island becomes heavily methylated, that gene is generally silenced: the methyl groups can physically block transcription factors from binding, or they can recruit proteins that read the methylation mark and recruit machinery to compact the surrounding chromatin. Conversely, an unmethylated CpG island at a promoter generally correlates with a gene that is actively being transcribed. This is the central rule to remember: more promoter methylation, less transcription.

What makes methylation genuinely heritable, and not just a one-time chemical event, is that it survives DNA replication. After the double helix is copied, the new strand is briefly unmethylated while the old template strand still carries its methyl marks, a state called hemimethylation. A maintenance methyltransferase recognizes this mismatched pattern and adds methyl groups to the new strand at the same positions, faithfully copying the parent cell's methylation pattern into both daughter cells. This is exactly the mechanism that lets epigenetic regulation, introduced in the previous section, persist stably across countless rounds of cell division.

DNA methylation shows up in several well-established biological phenomena: it is a key part of how one X chromosome is silenced in female mammalian cells, it enforces genomic imprinting by silencing the copy of certain genes inherited from one parent, and abnormal hypermethylation of tumor suppressor gene promoters is a recognized mechanism by which those protective genes get inappropriately shut off in cancer cells.
